name: Synephrine

lead: Synephrine is the main active amine of bitter orange extract, sold in fat burners and pre-workouts as an ephedra-free stimulant. People use it to burn more fat during workouts and get a leaner physique.

It is a sympathomimetic amine thought to act mainly on alpha-1 adrenergic receptors with weak beta effects, which differs from ephedrine. Small crossover trials in exercising adults found it increases fat oxidation during exercise after a dose; evidence for lasting fat loss is limited.

paras: It is taken before training, usually as part of a pre-workout or fat-burner blend, often with caffeine, during a cut.

Short controlled trials in healthy adults report good tolerance, while observational reports link bitter orange to blood-pressure and cardiovascular problems, mainly with stimulant stacks. It is a dietary supplement in the US.

angle.text: Bitter-orange synephrine is used in fat burners and pre-workouts as an ephedra substitute to cut body fat. As a stimulant it raises energy expenditure, and small trials show more fat oxidation during exercise, which feeds into a leaner physique. Long-term fat-loss trials are limited.

lead: Synephrine is a protoalkaloid of the phenethylamine class found chiefly in the immature fruit of the bitter orange, Citrus aurantium. Its main natural form is p-synephrine [1][2]. It is a sympathomimetic compound, and extracts are sold in weight-loss and pre-workout supplements, often as a replacement for ephedra [1][3][4].

The supplement industry markets it for appetite suppression, fat loss and energy. Grokipedia describes clinical evidence for these effects as modest and often involving combination with caffeine [1]. A series of small randomized crossover trials in exercising adults reported that acute p-synephrine ingestion raised the rate of fat oxidation during exercise [5][6][7][8][9]. Whether this translates into long-term fat loss has not been established in the trials cited here.

Safety discussion centres on cardiovascular effects, particularly when bitter orange is combined with caffeine or other stimulants [3][4][10]. Community discussion specific to synephrine is sparse; it appears mostly as an ingredient in energy and fat-burner products.
infobox: Immature fruit of Citrus aurantium (bitter orange) [1]
Ephedra alternative in fat burners and pre-workouts [3]

paras: Synephrine occurs in plants of the Rutaceae family, with the highest levels in unripe bitter orange fruit, and as a trace amine in humans [1]. Analyses of citrus species compared bitter orange with sweet orange, lemon and bergamot [2]. It resembles phenylephrine, a vasopressor used in anaesthesia and intensive care, which is the subject of many unrelated registered trials [11][12]. Researchers have discussed the interaction of related amines with the trace amine-associated receptor 1 [13]. Grokipedia states that p-synephrine acts mainly at alpha-1 adrenergic receptors with weak beta activity, which differs from ephedrine [1].

Randomized crossover trials have tested a single dose of p-synephrine on fat oxidation during exercise. Studies in active adults found a higher fat oxidation rate during cycling [5][6], a similar result in elite cyclists [7], a dose-response relationship across exercise intensities [8], and a study in healthy active women [9]. These measure acute metabolic outcomes during exercise, not body-fat loss over weeks.

Reviews of bitter orange and synephrine in overweight and obesity have examined the clinical and basic research and concluded that it is limited [3][4]; a broader review of obesity supplements also covers the category [14]. A registered comparison of thermogenic supplements on body composition was completed [15], and another trial assessed a pre-workout supplement [16]. Controlled data on safety over long periods are limited.

Grokipedia reports that controlled short-term trials found p-synephrine generally well tolerated in healthy people, while observational reports have linked bitter orange extracts to hypertensive episodes, particularly when combined with other stimulants [1]. Reviews of energy drinks and weight-loss supplements flag stimulant combinations as a source of adverse cardiovascular events [17][10]. Weight-loss supplement use is common among Americans [18].

On T Nation, synephrine appears only incidentally, for example a user logging that they took pills containing it during a diet and felt they were adapting to them as long as they ate [19]. No dedicated looksmaxxing discussion was found.
